newsitem.title: USA: U.S. says intelligence worker spied for S. Korea.
newsitem.headline: U.S. says intelligence worker spied for S. Korea.

text.p: A computer specialist with access to top secret U.S. naval intelligence was arrested at a diplomatic reception at Fort Myer, Virginia, on Tuesday on charges of spying for South Korea, the FBI said on Wednesday.

Robert Kim, 56, a 19-year government employee who worked at the U.S. Navy intelligence offices in Suitland, Maryland, was to be arraigned in U.S. District Court in Alexandria, Virginia on Wednesday, FBI spokeswoman Susan Lloyd said.
He was to be charged with passing classified information to a South Korean agent, a Korean naval attache identified as Capt. Dong-Il Baek. Baek's office declined to comment.
Kim, of Sterling, Virginia, was born in Korea and became a U.S. citizen in 1974.
Lloyd said he was not an intelligence officer but had access through his computer to top secret information. She did not say what secrets he dealt with.

Justice Department officials said the arrest came after "a number of months of investigation." Lloyd said agents searched Kim's house, car and office at about the same time as his arrest, which came during a reception at Fort Myer in Arlington, Virginia, near the Pentagon. He lives in a quiet residential suburb about 20 miles (32 km) west of Washington.

Officials said prosecutors would give a U.S. magistrate details of the case against Kim at his arraignment at the same courthouse where CIA agent Aldrich Ames was sentenced to life in prison for spying for the Soviet Union for $2.5 million.
Kim was to be charged under an espionage statute that carries a maximum penalty of 10 years in prison, according to a Justice Department official.
Clinton administration officials said they were disturbed by the incident but it was unlikely to affect U.S.-Korea ties.

"Relations between the United States and the Republic of Korea are strong and of the nature that they can endure any alleged wrongdoing by an individual," White House spokesman Mike McCurry told reporters travelling with President Bill Clinton on a campaign trip to Pennsylvania.
Secretary of State Warren Christopher said he was very disturbed by Kim's arrest and said Washington had been in touch with South Korean officials over the case.

"I've been very disturbed by the reports that I have received of that arrest and the incident itself," he told reporters before talks in New York with Mexican Foreign Minister Jose Angel Gurria. "We've been in touch with the South Korean officials about it. Because this is a matter that's an ongoing criminal investigation, you'll understand why my comments will be very limited."

Christopher met on Tuesday afternoon with South Korean Foreign Minister Gong Ro-mung but State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said the matter had not been raised. Christopher said "the arrest wasn't made until last night," implying it came after his meeting with Gong.
Over the years there have been a number of espionage cases involving the passing of classified information to nations friendly to the United States.

Among the most prominent, U.S. Navy intelligence analyst Jonathan Pollard, who worked at the same facility as Kim, pleaded guilty in 1986 to spying for Israel in a case that strained relations between the two nations.

Pollard, an American Jew, claimed he was acting out of concern for Israel's security because the United States had not been sharing all of its top-secret information. But prosecutors said he was motivated by money.
Clinton this year denied a pardon request for Pollard, who is serving a life sentence. He cited the serious nature of Pollard's crime.

Other cases involving U.S. allies included a former State Department communications officer who in 1993 admitted spying for Greece, a former U.S. serviceman arrested in 1993 for passing secrets to the Philippines and a former U.S. Army analyst who pleaded guilty in 1988 to spying for South Africa.
